name: MAX232ESE+T
title: MAX220-MAX249: +5 V multichannel RS-232 drivers and receivers
summary: A family of RS-232 line drivers and receivers for EIA/TIA-232E and V.28/V.24 links that run from a single +5 V supply. On-chip charge pumps double and invert the supply to about ±10 V, so no ±12 V rails are needed. Members range from two drivers and two receivers (MAX232, MAX232A and others) to eight drivers and ten receivers, with or without external capacitors, shutdown, receiver enables and receivers that keep listening in shutdown. The MAX232ESE+ is the MAX232 (two drivers, two receivers, four 1.0 µF pump capacitors) in a 16-pin narrow SO for -40 °C to +85 °C.
key_figures: ±5.0 V min, ±7.3 V typ into 3 kΩ (MAX223/MAX230-MAX241)
5 mA typ, 10 mA max, no load, 25 °C
0.8 V min low, 2.4 V max high, 0.5 V hysteresis typ

notes: A + suffix marks a lead(Pb)-free, RoHS-compliant package; dice (C/D) specifications come from the factory.
The military range 55°C to +125°C should read -55°C to +125°C.

operation.text: Each part holds up to four kinds of block: two charge pumps that make the RS-232 rails from +5 V, the line drivers, the line receivers, and the enable and shutdown inputs that control the last two.

The first pump uses C1 to double +5 V to about +10 V, stored on C3 at V+. The second uses C2 to turn that +10 V into about -10 V, stored on C4 at V-. These figures are for no load; the rails are not regulated and sag as current is drawn. The MAX225, MAX233, MAX235 and MAX245-MAX247 carry the pump capacitors inside and need no external parts; the MAX231 and MAX239 take V+ from a second supply and only invert it.

A little current may be taken from V+ and V- for other circuits, but not so much that a driver output drops below the ±5 V the RS-232 standard requires. V+ and V- are not brought out on the MAX225 and MAX245-MAX247. On parts with shutdown (MAX222, MAX225, MAX230, MAX235, MAX236, MAX240, MAX241, MAX245-MAX249) the rails should not feed other circuits: in shutdown V- drops to 0 V and V+ to +5 V.
When V+ is fed from an outside +10 V supply instead of the doubler, leave C1 out and tie SHDN to VCC, because in shutdown V+ is switched to VCC inside.

With VCC = +5 V and a nominal 5 kΩ receiver load, a driver swings about ±8 V. The ±5 V minimum of EIA/TIA-232E and V.28 is met in the worst case: 3 kΩ load, VCC = +4.5 V and the top of the temperature range. With no load the output reaches from about V+ - 1.3 V down to V- + 0.5 V. Inputs accept both TTL and CMOS levels. Slew rate stays under 30 V/µs as EIA/TIA-232E and V.28 demand; it is typically 24 V/µs with no load and 10 V/µs into 3 kΩ and 2500 pF.

Every driver input except on the MAX220 has a 400 kΩ pull-up to VCC sourcing about 12 µA, so an unused input may float: it sits high and, since the drivers invert, holds its output low. The pull-ups are switched off in shutdown. The MAX220 has none; its unused inputs go to GND or VCC.

In shutdown, in three-state, or with the supply removed, the driver outputs go high impedance and may be pulled to ±15 V. Leakage is typically a few microamperes and at most 25 µA; in low-power shutdown it is under 1 µA with the output at ground and stays under 1 µA when the output is driven anywhere from 0 V to VCC + 6 V. Below -0.5 V the output is clamped to ground by a diode, and near VCC + 6 V by a zener, each through about 1 kΩ. Supply current falls to about 8 µA in shutdown.

RS-232 counts a level above +3 V as logic 0, so every receiver inverts. The thresholds of 0.8 V and 2.4 V also let TTL levels drive the inputs. Each input takes up to ±25 V and has a nominal 5 kΩ termination to ground. The receivers follow the Type 1 reading of V.28 and EIA/TIA-232E fault conditions. Hysteresis is 0.5 V typical and at least 0.2 V, so slow or noisy edges still switch cleanly, and the delay is about 600 ns in either direction.

The MAX239 has a receiver three-state input; the MAX223, MAX225, MAX235, MAX236, MAX240 and MAX241 have that and a low-power shutdown input. On the MAX225, MAX235, MAX236 and MAX239-MAX241 the receiver outputs go high impedance while the three-state input is high, and also while shutdown is asserted. Table 2 sets out the combinations.

The MAX223, MAX242 and MAX245-MAX249 can shut down and still listen. The pumps and drivers stop, while enabled receivers keep working at reduced speed, so a sleeping system can be woken by activity on the line and then talk at full rate.

The MAX222, MAX235, MAX236, MAX240 and MAX241 disable every receiver in shutdown. On the MAX223 and MAX242 two receivers stay alive at reduced power: they act as CMOS inverters with no hysteresis, and the high-to-low input delay rises to about 2.5 µs. Those two parts also have a receiver output enable (active high EN on the MAX223, active low on the MAX242) that works apart from shutdown; on every other device the shutdown input (SHDN, or active-high SHDN on the MAX241) also turns the receiver outputs off.

The MAX243 has the MAX232A pinout but one of its two receivers lacks cable-fault protection. That receiver switches at about -0.8 V instead of +1.4 V, so its output goes high only when the input is actively driven negative; open, it reads as the 0 or clear-to-send state. The usual arrangement puts the data line (TD or RD) on the +1.4 V receiver and a handshake line (DTR, DSR, CTS, RTS) on the negative-threshold one, so a control line may be driven or left open and the same cable works with different equipment. On the other parts an input that is driven negative, open, or grounded sends the receiver output high, which tells the UART to stop sending; their handshake inputs therefore have to be driven or strapped to a positive level.

The MAX225 has five drivers and five receivers and the MAX245 eight drivers and ten receivers, each with separate transmitter and receiver enables. A high on ENT stops the pumps, puts the drivers in three-state and drops supply current below 25 µA, while the receivers run in low-power receive mode. On the MAX225 ENR controls all five receivers. On the MAX245 ENR controls RA1-RA4 and RB1-RB4, putting them in three-state when high; RA5 and RB5 are always active.

Receivers have three modes: full speed, three-state, and low-power receive (enabled receivers keep working at lower data rates). The receiver enables choose between full speed and three-state. Drivers have two modes, full speed and three-state, and the transmitter enables also control shutdown: once every transmitter is disabled the part shuts down and enabled receivers drop into low-power receive. Tables 1a-1d give every state; the MAX244 has no control pins.

Ten receivers, eight drivers and two control inputs, one per side. ENA high puts side A's four drivers and four receivers in three-state, ENB does the same for side B, and RA5 and RB5 stay active throughout. With both ENA and ENB at +5 V the whole part is in shutdown.

Nine receivers, eight drivers and four control inputs. ENRA and ENRB each control four receiver outputs, ENTA and ENTB four drivers each, and the ninth receiver, RB5, is always active. Both ENTA and ENTB high shut the part down.

Eight receivers, eight drivers and four control inputs: ENRA and ENRB control four receiver outputs each and ENTA and ENTB four drivers each. No receiver is always active. Both ENTA and ENTB high shut the part down with the drivers in three-state.

Ten receivers, six drivers and four control inputs: ENRA and ENRB control five receiver outputs each and ENTA and ENTB three drivers each, with no always-active receiver. Both ENTA and ENTB high give shutdown with the drivers in three-state, and active receivers then run in low-power receive mode at up to 20 kb/s.
Where supply noise matters, decouple VCC to ground with a capacitor equal in value to C1 and C2, placed as close to the device as possible.
